questions.worked_solution:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=4$ and vertical radius $b=2.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *outside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, $(5,0).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
4(5)^{2}+16(0)^{2}\,>\,64.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$
4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}>64.
$$

We must also include the curve $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}\ge 64.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}\ge 64\}.
$$

questions.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{x+5}{{x}^{2}-x-2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{2}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+5}{{x}^{2}-x-2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}})}{(1-\frac{1}{x}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{1}{x},\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}$ and $\frac{2}{{x}^{2}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{5}{{x}^{2}})}{(1-\frac{1}{x}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{1-0-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=A,$ what is the value of ${\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{4}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ A+{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Determine the area $A$ of the parallelogram spanned by $\text{u}=⟨5,-3⟩$ and $\text{v}=⟨-2,-4⟩.$

$\,\,A=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we construct a matrix where the columns are made up of the components of the corresponding vectors:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, we find the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot (-4)-(-2)\cdot (-3) \\  & =-20-6 \\  & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

The absolute value of $det(M)$ gives the area $A$ of the parallelogram:

$$
A=|\,-26\,|=26
$$

questions.problem: If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials of degree $13$ and $7$, respectively, what is the degree of $P+Q?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $P$ is a polynomial of degree $13,$ the leading term contains an ${x}^{13}.$

Since $Q$ is a polynomial of degree $7,$ the leading term contains an ${x}^{7}.$

In $P+Q,$ the highest-order term still contains an ${x}^{13}.$ No ${x}^{13}$ term in $Q$ could possibly cancel out the ${x}^{13}$ term in $P.$

Therefore, the degree of $P+Q$ must be $13.$
